utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber apologises for the late start, but the parties may understand that further preparations in the early morning hours are needed to deal with the matters which are on our desk at this moment; and also that it sometimes, despite the early start, takes more start than expected. I have an agenda on matters I will deal with before the first break, and then we might again have a bit of a longer break. Mr. Misetic, I was informed that you sent an e-mail that where we invited you to further give your priorities that you are available for the whole day, and the Chamber appreciates your availability, and it might have taken you quite some efforts to achieve this. I first start with, could I say, the painful things. That the is the Chamber made a mistake yesterday on the 3rd of March, and if I'm not mistaken it was at transcript page 17.085, with respect to D1439. The Chamber stated - but it was an error - that Exhibit D1439 was admitted into evidence. D1439 is a record of a statement taken of Witness 82, by the police administration in Zagreb, dated the 25th of May, 1998. The Chamber has heard oral submissions on the matter on the 27th of February, oral submissions in court with respect to the admission of this document; and once the Chamber had heard the submissions, also the submissions specifically by the Markac Defence, D1439 was included on the list of exhibits that were marked for identification. Again, the Chamber made a mistake and the status should change into tendered -- marked, not admitted. After the first break, the Chamber will give in further detail the reasons for the non-admission. Mr. Misetic, I think we still owe you an opportunity to respond to the Prosecution's motion to admit two documents on investigative steps taken by civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am still waiting for my team to get back to me on that. I asked them last night to take a look at that time. If I can have until after the first break, I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will leave it until after the first break. I hope this will not be the fate of most of the agenda items before the break. Then the Chamber has been informed about positions taken by the Gotovina and Markac Defence on the presidential transcripts. I just summarise from what I learned from the e-mails that were copied to the staff; that is, that the Gotovina Defence would like to add other transcripts of the same series; and to have added also two videos in -- which explain the position taken by Mr. Tudjman. I also took from the e-mails that you, Mr. Russo, that you would object against adding to this. I've now put this on the record because this is just a very short summary of what we learned the positions would be. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we're missing -- mixing two different issues up. I don't believe I got an e-mail from Mr. Russo indicating an objection to the presidential bar table or transcripts being bar tabled by us. I think that was a separate issue relating to P461 relating specifically to the Brioni transcript. And I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm mixing up the transcripts. Perhaps that's what happens if too much comes in. Therefore, it is good if we verify it on the record. Mr. Misetic is always right, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: He is correct, Your Honour. However, the Court is also correct, in fact, we will be objecting to the additional submissions of presidential transcripts by the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remember that I read something that it is not for the Defence at this moment to add -- to present evidence. Then I invited parties to put properly their positions on the recordings, and we start then, therefore, with exclusively the presidential transcript, not the Brioni one. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine although if I could I get copied of the Prosecution if something was sent to Chambers. I don't believe I received an e-mail stating their position so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit that I read a lot of e-mails in the early morning, and I might mix them up. I never noticed that we ever were copied on an e-mail which is not addressed to the Defence. Let me make that sure to the extent I may have confused matters, and I think the parties are perfectly aware of the guidelines that if it is relevant, if e-mail exchanges, we have three categories, the first of a purely practical nature, which do not necessarily have to reach the record; second category which is have some impact which will then be put on the record by referring to in a court session; and the third category are those of such impact that they should be filed, officially filed with the Registry. I am not aware that the Chamber was not copied on anything that was sent to the Defence. Let me make that clear. If I make a mistake there, then, please, correct me. But it is my understanding that the parties are fully aware of the rules that apply in these kind of e-mail communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I was just referring to I believe you made a comment there was some position taken that it's not for the Defence to be putting evidence and I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be clear. It could well be that this was comment or interpretation or understanding by the staff when having e-mail exchange with the Chamber that I would not conclude for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did not submit an e-mail to the Chamber, which was not copied to the Defence, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then next step, Mr. Misetic in relation to the presidential transcripts. I think your primary position was they should not be admitted [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The context is so narrow that it is impossible -- it is just taking a sentence and then not putting it in the proper context of the conversation. That's the first point. I specifically object with respect to the transcript with -- that has a comments made by General Gotovina on it as being inaccurately translated. And, therefore, before there is any admission we would ask, if the Chamber decides that it will admitted them, that a revised translations be done and circulated so that we can review them again. So if this had this been done at an appropriate time when witnesses still could be called and matters could be put to witness is, of course, always our preference to put matters to witnesses as well. Given that we are put in the position as a result of the late filing by the Prosecution of presidential transcripts, we then wish -- if the Chamber is inclined to admit five excerpts of presidential transcripts that the -- actually they're now two presidential transcripts because we did not realise that the Prosecution has not yet admitted the actual transcript from the 3rd of August where President Tudjman made the decision to launch Operation Storm. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. I take it that it was a slip of the tongue where you said that the Prosecution had not admitted yet sought to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First with respect to the presidential transcripts offered by the Prosecution if there is, in fact, a translation issue, we will certainly clear that up. Nevertheless, I don't believe that that should have any impact on admission into evidence. Likewise, I don't believe that the objections with respect to context should bar the admission of the presidential transcripts. The Defence is certainly free to put in any additional portions of those same transcripts which they feel would add context, and we certainly wouldn't object to that, nor would we object to putting in the full content of each of those transcripts; and the Defence can simply do as we have done and refer the Chamber to a particular portions of those transcripts however the Chamber feels is best to proceed. There is, however, an objection to admission of additional transcripts by the Gotovina Defence. These clearly not aimed at providing context to different conversations. It is presentation of their affirmative case, which should be done during their own case, simply because we haven't a bar table presidential transcripts at a certain point in time, doesn't entitle the Defence to put in their entire Defence case also by bar table. One of the transcripts they seek to put in is on the 65 ter list, so I don't know that there is an argument that they weren't in some way notified that that might be tendered into evidence. They certainly had the opportunity to put that or any other transcript, which had been disclosed to them to any witness who came into the case who could offer any evidence about it. But is it our position with respect to the two additional transcripts they wish to put in as well as the two videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is simply a question of fairness here. If these transcripts had come in through a live witness, we, in cross-examination, could have challenged the basis for which they were being tendered into evidence which has been put forward as proof of a JCE. In cross-examination, we could have put in counter-transcripts to refute the allegation of a JCE; and I see no reason, therefore, that if the Prosecution choosing instead of putting it to a live witness to bar table, that we in effect can have -- if you wish to call it this, a cross-examination bar table by putting in counter-evidence. It is simply a matter of direct and cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.text: I will not deal at this moment with P1050 up to and including P1118. So the first four we leave apart for a second. Then I move to P1167, P1168, P1174, and I -- in the same series, I will deal with a D exhibit we had not dealt with yet. That was D1212. The Chamber will give its designation on admission on these four documents, and I start with D1212: The Chamber denies the admission of D1212 and requests the Registrar to mark the document not admitted. The Chamber finds that the fact that an article of the New York Times stated in 1999 that, according to an internal report of the Prosecution, the Prosecution then decided during an internal meeting not to include the shelling of Knin in any indictment for whatever reason, does not go to proof of any matter that is to be decided by the Chamber in the present case. Further, the Chamber finds that D1212 does not contribute to the clarification of P1144, the conversation between Tudjman and Cermak on the 23rd of March, 1999. I now move to P1167, P1168, and P1174. With regard to these documents, the Chamber considers its order, pursuant to Rule 73 bis, under (D), to reduce the indictment, an order of the 21st of February, 2007. The Chamber noted in that order that the proposed reduction of the indictment was based on the understanding that the Prosecution, in relation to Rule 93 (A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, would be permitted to present relevant evidence relating to pattern, intent, or knowledge, and would lead evidence concerning, for example, testimony relating to crimes in charged municipalities that were part of a pattern of events encompassing the uncharged municipalities. The Chamber notes that although most of the observations of the Human Rights Action Teams mentioned in those documents were not made in the Split Military District or the Knin municipality but they were made within Sector South. More specifically, with regard to P1167, and P1168, the Chamber further considers that the observations mentioned in those documents concern, among other things, looting, burning, the conduct of Croatian soldiers, and the conduct of Croatian policemen. The Chamber, therefore, finds that these documents are relevant to a pattern of events relevant to the indictment. The Chamber, of course, will eventually consider the weight to be given to these documents. The Chamber admits P1167, P1168 into evidence and requests the Registrar to adjust the status of those documents, accordingly. With regard to P1174, the Chamber considers that the observations made by the Human Rights Action Teams mentioned in that document do relate to one event of two houses that were burned, but that the remainder of the document does not relate to events that are relevant to the indictment. The Chamber, therefore, finds that P1174 is not relevant to a pattern of events relevant to the indictment and does not admit it in evidence. The Chamber requests the Registrar to adjust the status of P1174 to marked, not admitted. P1251, expert report of Dr. Clark, either before or after the break I will read the decision the Chamber has reached. The same is true for P1291. And the same is true for P1292.

The filing of this motion so late in the Prosecution's case forced the Chamber to carefully balance various elements, particularly the following: That the Prosecution's last witness finished testifying yesterday, the 3rd of March, 2009, one week after the filing of the motion. On what date the Prosecution claimed to have come into possession of the material, to the extent that such information was provided, when the documents had been added to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list, if at all; whether the documents could have been tendered earlier; the volume of the material tendered; to what extent the proposed exhibits were repetitious of other material in evidence; whether it would be unfair to the Prosecution to proceed without admitting them into evidence; whether the Defence was given a fair chance to respond to the motion; and whether the material was appropriately tendered in a bar table submission, in light of the Chamber's previous guidance on this matter. This balancing exercise resulted in the decision to deny the motion in its entirety. The Chamber has decided to granted the motion to admit 28 documents and the -- and a video into evidence, and the reasons for this decision will follow. It depends on whether we'll have a session on the coming days or whether we'll not have a session, which may be of influence on whether the reason will be given orally or in writing. Then I would like to, as announced earlier this morning, I would like to give the reasons for the denial of admission into evidence of D1439. As the parties may remember, the decision yesterday, the wrong decision, but today corrected, was given this morning. These are these reasons not to admit Exhibit D1439. The Defence tendered D1439 primarily for the purpose of corroborating evidence given by Witness 82 in his testimony, regarding the witness's denial of the truthfulness of a newspaper interview. That newspaper interview was not tendered and, therefore, not admitted into evidence. As the statement at issue here was not taken for the purposes of those proceedings, it fell outside the provisions of Rule 92 ter of the Rules. Therefore, the Chamber considered whether, under Rule 89(C), the statement had sufficient probative value that it could be considered for admission. The Chamber found that D1439 lacked sufficient probative value for admission into evidence and that it was being tendered primarily in order to provide corroboration with respect to statements made by the witness in his testimony about an item, not admitted into evidence, the newspaper interview. The Chamber further found that, in any event, such corroborating evidence was unnecessary, in light of the testimony of the witness already given on the issue, and also found that in other respects, D1439 lacked sufficient probative value for the Chamber to exercise its discretion under Rule 89 (C) to allow its admission into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons. D1447 is apparently already marked as admitted into evidence, although it was MFI'd. D1447 is admitted into evidence, which in itself does not preclude the parties from considering procedural consequences of admission into evidence. Then the Chamber wants to deliver its decision on the admission of the expert report of Dr. Eric Baccard, which is MFI'd under P2314 and a decision on the Markac Defence motion not to admit certain parts of the first expert report. On the 28th of April, 2008, the Prosecution submitted two expert reports of Eric Baccard, pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 26th of May, the Gotovina Defence filed a notice under Rule 94 bis, in which it challenged the relevance of the reports, arguing that Eric Baccard did not perform the autopsies of the victims exhumed from sites in Korenica, Gracac, and Knin. On the 4th of February 2009, the Markac Defence filed a motion in which it requested the Chamber not to admit section 5.1 of the first report, arguing that the alleged killings contained in that section concern Korenica and fall outside the territorial scope of the indictment. On the 4th of February, 2009, the Prosecution tendered a redacted version of the first report, dated 6th of June, 2003, into evidence; and it was marked for identification as P2314. The general standards of admissibility set forth in Rule 89 of the Rules apply to expert reports. 89 (C) of the Rules provides that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. For a proposed expert report to be probative, the author should qualify as an expert in its subject matter, and the content of the expert report should fall within the accepted expertise of the witness. An expert is a person who, by virtue of some specialised knowledge, skill, or training can assist the trier of fact to understand or determine an issue in dispute. The Chamber notes that the expert status of the witness as such was not disputed by the Defence. On the basis of the redacted first expert report and the information on Eric Baccard's education and experience contained therein, and in P2313, the Chamber is satisfied that Eric Baccard qualifies as an expert in forensic pathology. The redacted first expert report comprises Eric Baccard's analysis of autopsy reports of bodies exhumed in 2002 from a site in Gracac, prepared by eight forensic pathologists. The Chamber finds that the matters addressed in the expert report are relevant to the indictment, in particular to the alleged murders charged as crime against humanity in Counts 1 and 6, and as violations of the laws and customs of war in Count 7. The Chamber further finds that the fact that Eric Baccard did not perform himself these autopsies does not affect the relevance of his expert report. The Chamber notes in particular that Eric Baccard was a member of the forensic monitoring team that attended, observed, and discussed the findings of the individual autopsy reports as indicated on transcript pages 15.748 through 15.751. When drafting his report, he had available to him the autopsy reports, his notes prepared at the various stages of the forensic examinations, and pictures of X-rays as shown on transcript pages 15.755 and onwards. The content of the report stays within the forensic pathological expertise of Eric Baccard. The Chamber further finds that the Markac Defence motion to exclude section 5.1 of the first expert report relating to bodies exhumed in Korenica has become moot since this section has been entirely redacted in the redacted version of the first expert report that was tendered by the Prosecution. Having read the report and considered the testimony of Eric Baccard, the Chamber finds that the redacted first expert report assists the Chamber in the understanding of the underlying forensic material. The Chamber, therefore, deems the report to have probative value. The Chamber is thus satisfied that it meets the requirements for admission set out in Rule 89 (C) of the Rules and the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. The Chamber, therefore, admits P2314, the redacted first expert report of Eric Baccard, into evidence. The Chamber also admits P2315, which is a signed list of autopsy reports that were available to Eric Baccard when he was preparing his expert report. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of the expert report of Eric Baccard and its decision on the Markac Defence motion not to admit certain parts of that report. utterances.text: Thank you. Then we move on. Second issue: Presidential transcripts. The Chamber will admit the presidential transcripts, the five portions, as tendered by the Prosecution. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the Chamber would avoid lengthy debates on how should upload it. The Prosecution further should consult with Mr. Misetic on the matter of translations, what makes a translation poor, what actually is the problem; and the Prosecution should then urgently prepare and for and organise how to get better translations uploaded and is invited to report on these efforts tomorrow, so that the Chamber has an idea when and how -- what the problem is and how it will be remedied. Then although I have a few more matters on my list, I'd prefer to read at least one and possibly two decisions. First decision is on the Markac motion to strike parts of the Theunens expert report and testimony. On the 17th of November, 2008, the Chamber issued its decision and guidance with regard to the expert report, addendum, and testimony of Reynaud Theunens. In its decision, the Chamber dealt with a number of arguments brought forward by the Gotovina Defence, joined by the Markac Defence, in its motion to strike Theunens's expert report and addendum. However, the Chamber deferred its final decision on admission of the expert report and addendum until after the testimony of Theunens. During his testimony, Theunens was extensively questioned by both parties, in relation to the production of his report, the content of the report, as well as his expertise. On the 11th of December, 2008, upon the conclusion of Theunens's testimony, the Chamber inquired with the parties whether there was a need for further submissions on the admission of the expert report, beyond those already dealt with in the Chamber's decision of the 17th of November, 2008. Neither the Prosecution nor the Defence expressed a need for making further submissions. This could be found at transcript page 13.530. On the 22nd of January, 2009, the Chamber admitted Theunens's expert report, the addendum, and the corrigendum into evidence as P1113, P1114 and P1115. This can be found on transcript page 14.865. On the same day, while the Court was sitting delivering its decision on admission the Markac Defence motion to strike portions of the Theunens's expert report and testimony was distributed to the Chamber. On the 4th of February, 2009, the Prosecution responded to the motion, arguing that it should be dismissed. On the 10th of February, 2009, the Markac Defence filed a request for leave to reply and a reply. The Chamber grants this request. In the motion, Markac Defence requests that certain portions of the Theunens' expert report not be admitted into evidence. However, the Markac Defence had failed to raise any objections to the admission either on the 11th of December, 2008, after invitation by the Chamber or at any later date, before the 22nd of January, 2009. The Markac Defence was aware that a housekeeping session when outstanding MFI's would be dealt with, was planned for this date. Nevertheless, it did not raise any objections before or at this session. In view of this, the Chamber considers that the Markac Defence had ample opportunity to raise any further objections to the admission of Theunens' expert report but failed to do so. The Chamber, therefore, proceeded to decide on the matter and this decision was issued on the 22 January, 2009. The Markac Defence has not requested certification to appeal the Chamber's decision. They have not asked the Chamber to exclude the expert report pursuant to Rule 95 of the Rules or requested to the Chamber to reconsider its decision on admission. The Theunens expert, therefore, is in evidence as of the 22nd of January, 2009, and remains in evidence. In its motion, the Markac Defence also requests the Chamber to strike Theunens' testimony with regard to certain topics that they claim do not fall within the witness's expertise. The Chamber understands this to mean that the Defence would like the Chamber to disregard these parts of the testimony. In its decision of the 17th of November, 2008, the Chamber set out that it was not necessary, at the admissibility stage, to scrutinise each opinion provided by the expert in the expert report, to ascertain whether it fell within the witness's expertise. Opinions that fall outside the expertise would simply be treated like other pieces of opinion evidence. They will not be automatically disregarded, but the Chamber will only consider whether to accept them as its own, if a proper basis for them has been demonstrated. The Chamber adopts the same approach with regard to Theunens' viva voce testimony. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber denies the Markac Defence motion. And this concludes the Chamber's decision.
